title: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
hook: an Eastern Catholic church outlawed under Soviet rule that survived underground

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world Church: on every continent, its center of gravity moving. Your line was the church moved south. What did you learn about the Church somewhere you've never been? Today, a church that had to go under the ground. Day nine hundred forty-three.

A small apartment in Soviet Ukraine, late at night, the curtains drawn. A man who spends his days as a laborer takes a folded cloth from a drawer, spreads it on the kitchen table, and sets out bread and a cup. A few neighbors have come in quietly, one at a time, so no one notices a crowd. He is a priest, and this is the Divine Liturgy, sung almost in a whisper. Accounts from those years describe scenes like this. Officially, his church does not exist. Today is the church that kept existing anyway.
screen: `CURTAINS DRAWN, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `A KITCHEN TABLE FOR AN ALTAR.` → `A CHURCH THAT DOESN'T EXIST.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church worships the way Orthodox Christians in Ukraine do: icons, incense, the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, married men among its parish priests. And it is in full communion with the pope. Greek in its name means the Byzantine tradition, not the country. It is one of the Eastern Catholic churches, which keep their own rites and their own laws while belonging to the one Catholic Church. Second, the ban. After the Second World War, Soviet authorities set out to erase it. Its bishops were arrested. A gathering held under state pressure declared the church dissolved and its parishes joined to the Russian Orthodox Church. Priests who refused were sent to labor camps. Its head, Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj, spent years in the camps before he was released to Rome. Third, the underground. The church didn't vanish. It went into kitchens, forests and cemeteries. Bishops were ordained in secret. Priests held ordinary jobs and served at night. Grandmothers baptized babies quietly and taught the prayers at home. Catholics read those years through a promise in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." A kitchen table was enough. Fourth, the return. As Soviet rule loosened toward its end, the church came out of hiding, and its people filled their churches openly again. It's a story with wounds on more than one side: Orthodox believers suffered under the same regime, and churches in Ukraine still carry that history together. But the underground church kept the Liturgy going in the dark until it could sing it in daylight.
screen: `EASTERN WORSHIP, IN COMMUNION WITH ROME.` · `DECLARED DISSOLVED BY THE STATE.` · `KITCHENS, FORESTS AND CEMETERIES.` · `OUT OF HIDING, INTO DAYLIGHT.` · then, large: `THERE AM I IN THE MIDST OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe with both lungs. John Paul the Second liked to say the Church has to breathe with both its lungs, East and West. Settle, and take a slow breath, and notice it fill both sides of your chest. Keep breathing that way. With each breath, let one of the Eastern Catholic churches come to mind, even if all you know is a name: Ukrainian, Melkite, Maronite, Syro-Malabar, and others, some of them living through war or exile right now. If you pray, you can pray for them on each breath. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, one breath each. The bell holds the time.
The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. An Eastern Catholic church of the Byzantine tradition, in communion with Rome, outlawed under Soviet rule, that survived underground.

segments.voice: Your line: the underground church. Today, notice one faithful thing someone keeps doing where nobody sees it, and thank them if you can. Day nine hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Ukrainian Greek Catholics celebrate the Byzantine Divine Liturgy in Ukrainian and other languages, in Ukraine and in parishes abroad, and honor the bishops, priests and laypeople who were imprisoned or killed under Soviet rule.
